script.opening: "Doctor, I’ve had these really itchy purple bumps come up on the insides of my wrists and my shins — they’ve got tiny white lines on them. And now the inside of my cheeks has gone sore with white lacy streaks. What is this, and is it serious?"

facts.text: About 6 weeks. Small flat-topped shiny purple bumps on the inner wrists and both shins; some have joined into patches. Fine white lines on top. New ones came up along a scratch on her arm. The itch is intense, worst at night. Will show the wrists to the camera.

Inside of both cheeks sore for about 3 weeks, especially with spicy food or tomatoes. White lacy streaks she has seen in the mirror. No ulcer that hasn’t healed, no lump, no red patches she has noticed. Teeth fine; sees the dentist yearly.
Nails: "a couple look ridged". Scalp fine, no hair loss. Some itching and soreness "down below" — only if asked directly and sensitively.
Bendroflumethiazide 2.5 mg for blood pressure for 2 years — "nothing new". Occasional ibuprofen. No allergies.
Generally well, no fevers. No liver problems known. No tattoos, never injected drugs, no blood transfusions. Non-smoker; drinks a glass or two of wine at weekends.
Works as a legal secretary. Married, two teenage children. Worried about passing it on to the family.

Calm but worried, scratching your wrists during the call. Ask whether it is catching and whether a strong steroid is safe. Be relieved by a clear name and explanation; promise to see the dentist if advised.

ice.ideas: "I wondered if it was something catching — or an allergy."
ice.concerns: "Because it’s in my mouth too, I’m scared it’s something serious — my friend had mouth cancer." The itch is ruining her sleep.
ice.expectations: "Know what it is and stop the itching."

cues: "The itch is intense" — impact on sleep; needs effective treatment.
"It’s in my mouth too — is it serious?" — fear of cancer and the need for long-term mouth checks.
"Blood pressure tablet for a couple of years" (if medicines are asked) — a possible drug trigger.

checkpoints.text: Recognises LICHEN PLANUS from the 6 Ps (pruritic, planar, polygonal, purple papules) with Wickham striae on flexor wrists/ankles/shins
Looks for ORAL (white lacy/reticular, sometimes erosive) and nail/scalp/genital involvement and the Koebner phenomenon
Considers a drug-induced LICHENOID eruption (reviews medications) and the hepatitis C association with oral lichen planus
Manages with POTENT TOPICAL CORTICOSTEROIDS first-line (+ antihistamines/emollients; topical steroids for oral LP) and refers dermatology for extensive/erosive/nail-scalp-scarring/refractory disease

Counsels the usually self-limiting course and notes the SMALL malignant-transformation (SCC) risk of ORAL LP (about 1% over 10 years, BAD) and erosive genital LP, arranging monitoring/dental review and knowing the NICE NG12 oral criteria
Reassures appropriately (not serious/not contagious), addresses the itch and the sore mouth, and checks understanding
Explains the diagnosis and plan accessibly without over-alarming about the malignancy note

Safety-nets and follows up: review of itch/response, long-term dental/specialist monitoring for the oral disease (about 1% risk over 10 years), drug/hep C review, and when to return — correct naming + treatment + appropriate monitoring

worked.txt: (After seeing the skin and mouth in person.) "This is lichen planus — the itchy, flat-topped purple bumps with those fine white lines, and the lacy white streaks in your mouth, are typical. It’s not cancer and it’s not contagious, so let me reassure you on that."
"For the bumps, a strong steroid cream usually settles them and the itch, plus an antihistamine and good moisturiser. For your mouth, a steroid mouthwash or paste and gentle oral care help."

"Let me check your medicines, as a few tablets can trigger a similar rash — including your water tablet — and, if you agree, I’ll arrange a blood test for hepatitis C, which is occasionally linked to lichen planus in the mouth."
"The skin version usually fades over months — sometimes leaving a brownish mark for a while — and can occasionally come back. The mouth type can be more persistent."

"One reason I want to keep an eye on the mouth: lichen planus there carries a small risk of changing over time — about 1 in 100 over ten years — so I’d like your dentist to review it regularly, and any ulcer lasting more than three weeks or a red patch needs checking quickly. Nothing to panic about, just sensible monitoring."
"Come back if it spreads a lot, the mouth becomes very sore or ulcerated, your nails or scalp get involved, or it’s not settling — then I’d involve a skin specialist."

f.learning: LICHEN PLANUS is recognised by the classic "6 Ps" — PRURITIC, PLANAR (flat-topped), POLYGONAL, PURPLE/violaceous PAPULES/plaques — with fine white surface lines (WICKHAM STRIAE), favouring the flexor wrists, ankles and shins, and often with ORAL involvement (white lacy/reticular, sometimes erosive streaks) and sometimes nail (ridging/pterygium), SCALP (scarring alopecia/lichen planopilaris) and GENITAL disease, with Koebner phenomenon at trauma sites. Consider a drug-induced LICHENOID eruption (thiazides, antimalarials, beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs — review medications) and the recognised association of oral lichen planus with HEPATITIS C. Manage cutaneous LP with POTENT (or very potent) TOPICAL CORTICOSTEROIDS first-line (BAD 2024; PCDS) plus antihistamines/emollients for itch, and oral LP with topical steroids and oral hygiene; refer to dermatology for extensive, erosive, nail/scalp-scarring or refractory disease. Counsel that cutaneous lichen planus is usually SELF-LIMITING over months to ~1–2 years (may leave post-inflammatory pigmentation) but can recur, and note that ORAL lichen planus carries a SMALL risk of malignant transformation (SCC) — about 1% over 10 years (BAD) — and erosive genital disease also needs follow-up, warranting monitoring and dental/specialist review; NICE NG12: unexplained oral ulceration for more than 3 weeks, or a lump or red/red-and-white patch, needs referral. Reassure (not serious/not contagious), treat the itch, review drugs/associations, and arrange appropriate monitoring.

knowledge.summary: Intensely itchy, flat-topped, violet papules with fine white lines on the wrists and shins, together with white lacy streaks on the inner cheeks, is lichen planus. Treat the skin with a potent topical steroid, check her medicines for a lichenoid drug reaction, consider hepatitis C testing, and arrange dental or oral medicine follow-up because sore oral lichen planus carries a small long-term cancer risk.

points.t: Itchy, shiny, flat-topped, polygonal, purple (violaceous) papules, often with fine white lines on the surface (Wickham striae), typically on the flexor wrists, forearms, shins and ankles [1][3]. New lesions can appear in scratches or scars (Koebner phenomenon). It heals leaving brown marks, especially in darker skin.

Mouth: white lacy (reticular) streaks on the inner cheeks, sometimes red, sore or ulcerated (erosive) [2]. Also ask about and look at the nails (thinning, ridging, pterygium), scalp (patchy hair loss with scarring, lichen planopilaris) and, sensitively, the genitals, where erosive disease can scar. These sites need earlier specialist input.

Most cases have no identifiable cause [1]. Review all medicines, including over-the-counter ones: a lichenoid drug eruption can look identical, and culprit drugs include some antihypertensives, antimalarials and gold. Some oral lichen planus is linked to chronic hepatitis C [2], so consider testing with consent. Dental amalgam next to oral lesions can cause a local lichenoid reaction.

A potent or very potent topical steroid is usually needed, because lichen planus often does not respond to weaker ones [1][5]; use a moderate one in skin folds. Add emollients and a sedating antihistamine at night if itch disturbs sleep (doses per BNF). Widespread, severe or resistant disease needs dermatology (phototherapy or systemic treatment).

Topical steroids as mouthwashes, sprays or pastes help most people with oral lichen planus [2]; choice and dose per BNF or oral medicine advice. Avoid foods that sting, keep teeth and gums healthy with regular dental care, and stop smoking and limit alcohol, which also reduces oral cancer risk.
Skin lichen planus usually settles over months to a year or two, though it can recur [1]. Oral lichen planus tends to last longer, often for years [2].

BAD [2]: oral lichen planus carries about a 1% risk of cancerous change over 10 years, so long-term review by a dentist or oral medicine team is advised. Erosive genital lichen planus also needs specialist follow-up. NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for unexplained oral ulceration lasting more than 3 weeks, and an urgent dental referral for a lump, or a red or red and white patch consistent with erythroplakia or erythroleukoplakia.
Lichen planus is not infectious and cannot be passed on [1]. Say so early; it is a common unspoken worry.

model.text: Hello Mrs Forsyth, I’m Dr Nwosu. Come in. What can I do for you today?

Doctor, I’ve had these really itchy purple bumps come up on the insides of my wrists and my shins. They’ve got tiny white lines on them. And now the inside of my cheeks has gone sore with white lacy streaks. What is this, and is it serious?
That sounds miserable, and I can see why you want answers. I’ll ask a few questions, take a proper look, and then explain what I think it is.
How long have the bumps been there, and how bad is the itch? Is it affecting your sleep?
I couldn’t give you an exact date. The itch is intense, though. It’s the worst part.
And your mouth: is it sore all the time or with certain foods? Any ulcers or raw areas that don’t heal?
model.why: Screens erosive disease and non-healing ulceration (NICE NG12)

model.text: It’s sore, especially when I eat. I haven’t noticed ulcers as such.
Have you noticed any changes in your nails, patches of hair loss on your scalp, or any soreness in the genital area? I ask because this kind of rash can affect those places too.
model.why: Nail, scalp and genital involvement asked sensitively

model.text: Not that I’ve noticed.
Have you started any new medicines, including anything from the chemist, in the last few months?
No, nothing new.
Any other health problems I should know about, for example liver problems?
No, I’m generally well.
What have you been thinking it might be?
I didn’t know. I wondered if it was something catching, or something serious because it’s in my mouth too.
Those are really fair worries. What were you hoping we could do today?
Know what it is and stop the itching.

May I look at your wrists, shins and inside your mouth? … These are flat-topped, shiny purple bumps with fine white lines on top, and inside your cheeks there’s a white lacy pattern. I’ll also look at your nails and scalp while I’m here.
model.why: Examines skin, mouth, nails, scalp with consent

model.text: What is it then?

This is lichen planus. It’s a condition where the immune system causes inflammation in the skin and the lining of the mouth. The pattern you have is typical. It isn’t catching, you can’t pass it on to anyone, and it isn’t cancer.
model.why: Names diagnosis; addresses contagion and cancer worries

model.text: That’s a relief. Will it go away?
On the skin it usually settles over months, sometimes a year or two, and it can leave brownish marks that fade slowly. In the mouth it tends to last longer.

For the skin, a strong steroid ointment works best, because weaker ones often don’t touch it. You apply it just to the bumps, and I’ll tell you how long to use it for. A good moisturiser helps, and an antihistamine at night can help you sleep.
model.why: Potent topical steroid, emollient, sedating antihistamine

model.text: Is a strong steroid safe?
Used on these spots for a limited time, yes. Thinning of the skin comes with long use on the same area, which is why we plan the course and review it. I wouldn’t use it on your face or in skin folds.
model.why: Addresses steroid fear with a balanced answer

model.text: Okay. And my mouth?

For the mouth there are steroid mouthwashes or sprays that help most people. Avoiding spicy food and keeping your teeth and gums healthy helps too. I’d also like your dentist to keep an eye on it over time. In a small number of people, about 1 in 100 over ten years, long-standing mouth lichen planus can change into a cancer, so regular checks are sensible, not a reason to panic.
model.why: Oral treatment and honest, proportionate cancer-risk counselling

model.text: I’ll make sure I go.

Two more things. I’d like to offer a blood test for hepatitis C, because it’s occasionally linked with this in the mouth. It’s a routine check, not because I think you’re at risk. Is that okay? And if you smoke or drink much, cutting down helps protect the mouth.
model.why: Hepatitis C testing with consent; modifiable oral cancer risks

model.text: Yes, that’s fine.

Come back if any mouth ulcer or sore patch doesn’t heal within three weeks, if you notice a lump or a red patch in your mouth, if your nails or scalp are affected, or if the skin isn’t improving after the steroid course. I’ll see you in about a month to check how it’s going.
So: strong cream on the spots, mouthwash, blood test, dentist checks, and come back if anything in my mouth doesn’t heal.
Exactly. And remember, it isn’t catching.
Thank you. That’s really put my mind at rest.

social.t: Severe itch disrupts sleep and concentration. Asking about impact helps target treatment such as a night-time antihistamine.
Visible purple patches and marks afterwards can cause embarrassment; saying clearly that it is not contagious helps at work and socially.

legal.t: GMC Decision making and consent (2020): explain why a hepatitis C test is offered and what a positive result would mean before testing.

professional.t: Long-term oral lichen planus review usually sits with the dentist or oral medicine. Write it into the plan and check she has access to a dentist.
Prescribe potent steroids with clear instructions on where, how much and for how long, and review, following the BNF potency guidance.

community.t: If she has no dentist, NHS 111 or local dental access services can help her find one for monitoring.
BAD patient information leaflets on lichen planus and oral lichen planus give reliable written information to take away.

redFlags: Mouth ulcer or sore area not healing after 3 weeks (NICE NG12)
Red or red and white patch, or a lump, in the mouth
Scalp hair loss with scarring or nail destruction
psychosocial: Access to a dentist for long-term review
ice: Idea: something catching, or serious because it is in the mouth
Expectation: a diagnosis and relief from the itch

playbook.diagnosis: “This is lichen planus: the itchy, flat-topped purple bumps with fine white lines on your wrists and shins, and the lacy white pattern in your cheeks, are typical.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your immune system is causing inflammation in the top layer of the skin and the lining of the mouth. It’s not an infection and it can’t be passed on. On the skin it usually burns itself out over months.”

management.reflectIce: “You wondered if it was catching or serious because it’s in your mouth. It isn’t catching and it isn’t cancer, but the mouth deserves regular checks.”
management.psychosocial: Address sleep and itch; reassure about contagion; check dental access; explain steroid safety.
sharedPlan: Potent topical steroid to skin lesions, moderate in folds; emollient; sedating antihistamine at night (per BNF)
Topical steroid mouthwash or spray for the mouth; avoid irritant foods; good oral hygiene
Review medicines for lichenoid drug eruption; hepatitis C test with consent
Dental or oral medicine long-term review; dermatology if extensive, erosive, nail or scalp scarring, or not responding
safetyNet: Return if any oral ulcer or patch persists beyond 3 weeks, or a lump or red patch appears
Return if nails, scalp or genitals become involved
Review in about a month for response
Regular dental checks for oral disease

pitfalls.intro: The trap is treating the itch as eczema and missing the mouth. The marks sit in naming lichen planus, treating it at the right strength, and setting up proportionate oral follow-up.

items.why: BAD: lichen planus often does not respond to weaker steroids.
items.fix: Potent topical steroid to the lesions with clear instructions and review.

items.fail: Not looking in the mouth, at the nails or the scalp.
items.why: Other sites change management and follow-up.
items.fix: Examine them and ask about genital symptoms sensitively.

items.why: A lichenoid drug eruption looks identical and settles when the drug is stopped.
items.fix: Ask about all medicines, including over-the-counter ones.

items.fail: No plan for the oral disease.
items.why: BAD: about 1% risk of cancerous change over 10 years; NICE NG12 sets criteria for non-healing ulcers and red patches.
items.fix: Dental or oral medicine review and a 3-week non-healing safety-net.

items.fail: Missing her worry that it is catching.
items.why: It is a common unspoken fear.
items.fix: “It isn’t catching, and you can’t pass it on.”

items.why: Potent steroids need review and response should be checked.
items.fix: Review in about a month; clear return criteria.

Duration, itch and sleep, mouth soreness and non-healing ulcers, nails, scalp, genital symptoms, new medicines, liver history.
Is it catching? Is it serious because it is in the mouth? Wants a name and relief.
Skin, mouth, nails, scalp. Lichen planus; not contagious; not cancer; the likely course.
Potent steroid, antihistamine, oral steroid preparation, dental follow-up with the 1% figure, hepatitis C test, NICE NG12 safety-net, review in a month.

wordPics.fail: Calls it eczema and gives hydrocortisone; never looks in the mouth or asks about medicines; either ignores the oral cancer risk or frightens her with it; no follow-up.
wordPics.pass: Recognises lichen planus, gives a potent topical steroid, treats the mouth, reviews medicines, reassures that it is not contagious, and arranges dental follow-up.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: checks nails, scalp and genital symptoms sensitively; explains the cancer risk as a proportionate figure; offers hepatitis C testing with a clear reason; gives an NICE NG12-aligned mouth safety-net; addresses steroid worries; teach-back and review date.

avoid.dont: “It’s just a bit of eczema, try hydrocortisone.”
avoid.instead: “This is lichen planus, and it usually needs a strong steroid ointment.”
avoid.why: Mild steroids rarely control lichen planus; the diagnosis also changes follow-up.

avoid.dont: “Mouth lichen planus can turn into cancer.”
avoid.instead: “About 1 in 100 over ten years, so we keep an eye on it with regular dental checks.”
avoid.why: An unquantified cancer warning frightens without helping her act.

avoid.dont: “We should test you for hepatitis because of your lifestyle.”
avoid.instead: “It’s occasionally linked with this rash, so I offer the test routinely.”
avoid.why: Explains the reason without implying judgement.

points.t: Itchy, shiny, flat-topped, polygonal, purple (violaceous) papules, often with fine white lines on the surface (Wickham striae), typically on the flexor wrists, forearms, shins and ankles [1][3]. New lesions can appear in scratches or scars (Koebner phenomenon). It heals leaving brown marks, especially in darker skin.

Mouth: white lacy (reticular) streaks on the inner cheeks, sometimes red, sore or ulcerated (erosive) [2]. Also ask about and look at the nails (thinning, ridging, pterygium), scalp (patchy hair loss with scarring, lichen planopilaris) and, sensitively, the genitals, where erosive disease can scar. These sites need earlier specialist input.

Most cases have no identifiable cause [1]. Review all medicines, including over-the-counter ones: a lichenoid drug eruption can look identical, and culprit drugs include some antihypertensives, antimalarials and gold. Some oral lichen planus is linked to chronic hepatitis C [2], so consider testing with consent. Dental amalgam next to oral lesions can cause a local lichenoid reaction.

A potent or very potent topical steroid is usually needed, because lichen planus often does not respond to weaker ones [1][5]; use a moderate one in skin folds. Add emollients and a sedating antihistamine at night if itch disturbs sleep (doses per BNF). Widespread, severe or resistant disease needs dermatology (phototherapy or systemic treatment).

Topical steroids as mouthwashes, sprays or pastes help most people with oral lichen planus [2]; choice and dose per BNF or oral medicine advice. Avoid foods that sting, keep teeth and gums healthy with regular dental care, and stop smoking and limit alcohol, which also reduces oral cancer risk.
Skin lichen planus usually settles over months to a year or two, though it can recur [1]. Oral lichen planus tends to last longer, often for years [2].

BAD [2]: oral lichen planus carries about a 1% risk of cancerous change over 10 years, so long-term review by a dentist or oral medicine team is advised. Erosive genital lichen planus also needs specialist follow-up. NICE NG12: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for unexplained oral ulceration lasting more than 3 weeks, and an urgent dental referral for a lump, or a red or red and white patch consistent with erythroplakia or erythroleukoplakia.
Lichen planus is not infectious and cannot be passed on [1]. Say so early; it is a common unspoken worry.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let her describe skin and mouth fully before asking.
Sleep disturbed by itch; worry about infecting others; ability to attend dental reviews.
Picked up “tiny white lines” (Wickham striae) and the mouth changes as one diagnosis.
Idea (catching, or serious because of the mouth), concern (cancer), expectation (a name and relief from itch).
Examined skin, mouth, nails and scalp with consent; offered hepatitis C test; biopsy or specialist review if uncertain.
Lichen planus versus lichenoid drug eruption, eczema, psoriasis, oral candidiasis or leukoplakia.
Screened for non-healing oral ulceration and red patches (NICE NG12); erosive and genital disease.
Lichen planus of skin and oral mucosa.
Potent topical steroid for skin, emollient, antihistamine; topical steroid for mouth; dental or oral medicine follow-up; hepatitis C test.
Medicines reviewed for lichenoid reaction; smoking and alcohol advice; steroid safety concerns addressed.
Return if oral ulcer or patch persists beyond 3 weeks, nails or scalp involved, or no response; review in about a month.

social.t: Severe itch disrupts sleep and concentration. Asking about impact helps target treatment such as a night-time antihistamine.
Visible purple patches and marks afterwards can cause embarrassment; saying clearly that it is not contagious helps at work and socially.

legal.t: GMC Decision making and consent (2020): explain why a hepatitis C test is offered and what a positive result would mean before testing.

professional.t: Long-term oral lichen planus review usually sits with the dentist or oral medicine. Write it into the plan and check she has access to a dentist.
Prescribe potent steroids with clear instructions on where, how much and for how long, and review, following the BNF potency guidance.

community.t: If she has no dentist, NHS 111 or local dental access services can help her find one for monitoring.
BAD patient information leaflets on lichen planus and oral lichen planus give reliable written information to take away.

redFlags: Mouth ulcer or sore area not healing after 3 weeks (NICE NG12)
Red or red and white patch, or a lump, in the mouth
Scalp hair loss with scarring or nail destruction
psychosocial: Access to a dentist for long-term review
ice: Idea: something catching, or serious because it is in the mouth
Expectation: a diagnosis and relief from the itch

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is lichen planus: the itchy, flat-topped purple bumps with fine white lines on your wrists and shins, and the lacy white pattern in your cheeks, are typical.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your immune system is causing inflammation in the top layer of the skin and the lining of the mouth. It’s not an infection and it can’t be passed on. On the skin it usually burns itself out over months.”

management.reflectIce: “You wondered if it was catching or serious because it’s in your mouth. It isn’t catching and it isn’t cancer, but the mouth deserves regular checks.”
management.psychosocial: Address sleep and itch; reassure about contagion; check dental access; explain steroid safety.
sharedPlan: Potent topical steroid to skin lesions, moderate in folds; emollient; sedating antihistamine at night (per BNF)
Topical steroid mouthwash or spray for the mouth; avoid irritant foods; good oral hygiene
Review medicines for lichenoid drug eruption; hepatitis C test with consent
Dental or oral medicine long-term review; dermatology if extensive, erosive, nail or scalp scarring, or not responding
safetyNet: Return if any oral ulcer or patch persists beyond 3 weeks, or a lump or red patch appears
Return if nails, scalp or genitals become involved
Review in about a month for response
Regular dental checks for oral disease

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The trap is treating the itch as eczema and missing the mouth. The marks sit in naming lichen planus, treating it at the right strength, and setting up proportionate oral follow-up.

items.why: BAD: lichen planus often does not respond to weaker steroids.
items.fix: Potent topical steroid to the lesions with clear instructions and review.

items.fail: Not looking in the mouth, at the nails or the scalp.
items.why: Other sites change management and follow-up.
items.fix: Examine them and ask about genital symptoms sensitively.

items.why: A lichenoid drug eruption looks identical and settles when the drug is stopped.
items.fix: Ask about all medicines, including over-the-counter ones.

items.fail: No plan for the oral disease.
items.why: BAD: about 1% risk of cancerous change over 10 years; NICE NG12 sets criteria for non-healing ulcers and red patches.
items.fix: Dental or oral medicine review and a 3-week non-healing safety-net.

items.fail: Missing her worry that it is catching.
items.why: It is a common unspoken fear.
items.fix: “It isn’t catching, and you can’t pass it on.”

items.why: Potent steroids need review and response should be checked.
items.fix: Review in about a month; clear return criteria.
